title: Disney Files Patents for AI That Form Emotional Bonds Using Guest Memories
content:
Update: this article was updated to include a “sister” patent with similar technology, which was filed on the same date.
Disney has filed two patents for emotionally responsive AI interactive characters, possibly creating a way for a more emotional and personal interaction with characters in the future.
Emotionally Responsive AI Interactive Character Patents
The first patent, filed by Disney Enterprises on June 29, 2026, describes an AI-powered character that can use the memories of a guest and emotional context to make interactions feel more personal.
The abstract reads:
There is provided a method including eliciting, via an artificial intelligence interactive character (AIIC), a reminiscence from a user, predicting, using a trained machine learning (ML) model, at least one user memory feature from the reminiscence, computing, for each memory node of the plurality of memory nodes, a bond factor between the predicted at least one user memory feature and the one or more memory features stored in the memory node to provide a plurality of bond factors, determining that none of the plurality of bond factors satisfies a threshold, and in response to determining that none of the plurality of bond factors satisfies the threshold: updating the memory data structure by inserting a new memory node storing the predicted at least one user memory feature in the memory data structure; and generating, using the updated memory data structure, an interactive communication for execution by the AlIC. 1
Essentially, the technology will allow a character to respond to more than just a question or statement by the guest. It asks the guest to share a memory, and the AI model considers the people, places, activities, and emotional states of the memory. The technology compares the guest’s experience to the character’s experience (which come from a “memory bank”) to create a response. This may include speech, facial expressions, or movements.
If there is no relevant memory to match, the character makes up a new one that gets added to the memory bank. The patent itself calls this a “hallucinated memory,” but it’s more improvising a backstory instead of lying to guests.
AI Generated Creative Content Based on Shared Memories Patent
The second patent was published on the same date by an overlapping team. It uses the same memory-matching system, where the character draws a memory out of the guest, compares it with its own backstory, and finds a close match to create a response.
However, instead of holding a conversation with the guest like in the other patent, this patent describes that the character writes and performs a song, poem, or dance based on those memories. The AI-generated music has not been of the same caliber when compared to human-composed work.
The abstract reads:
There is provided a system including a computing platform having a hardware processor and a system memory storing a software code and a memory data structure storing memory features for an artificial intelligence interactive character (AIIC). The hardware processor is configured to execute the software code to elicit, using the AIIC, a reminiscence from a user, predict, using a trained machine learning model and the reminiscence, at least one user memory feature, identify, using the memory data structure, one or more of the memory features for the AIIC based on a similarity between the predicted at least one user memory feature and the memory features for the AIIC, determine a mood modifier based on emotion information of the identified one or more of the memory features for the AIIC, and generate a creative composition for performance by the AIIC based on the mood modifier.
To get into a bit more detail about what the patent describes, after the character receives the memory from the guest, it matches the memory to its own memory bank, picks a song structure, creates lyrics, composes chords and a melody, and then performs the song, poem, or dance.
If put in use, these patents could create more personable and unique interactions with robotic, animated, and other types of characters in the parks and in other environments instead of scripted interactions. We may or may not ever see this technology put to use, and if we do it could be years. Disney has not made any announcements related to these patents.
Other patents recently published by Disney describe possible improvements to real-time motion capture for animated projects, automatic removal of crowds and other unwanted background elements from photos, and the technology for the “HoloTile Floor.”
What do you think of these patents? Let us know on social media.

report.summary: Disney filed two patents for AI park characters that draw out guests' spoken memories to build emotional bonds and generate personalized songs, poems, or dances.
report.background: Disney's character interactions remain largely scripted: meet-and-greets run on fixed dialogue, cast-member training, and safety rules. Meanwhile, large language models, persistent memory architectures, affective computing, and free-roaming animatronics (Disney's own HoloTile floor, GD-I style robots, motion-capture patents) have matured quickly. The two patents, filed June 29, 2026, describe a shared architecture: a character elicits a reminiscence from a guest, a trained ML model extracts memory features such as people, places, activities, and emotional states, and the system scores those features against the character's own 'memory bank' to compute a 'bond factor.' When no stored memory clears a threshold, the character improvises a new backstory memory and writes it into the bank. This mirrors the wider industry shift toward long-term memory and emotional personalization in consumer AI, where retention depends on feeling known rather than on raw model capability.
key_points: Memory matching is the core mechanic: the AI character asks a guest to recall something, a machine learning model extracts features like people, places, activities, and feelings, then compares them against the character's stored 'memory nodes.' Each comparison produces a 'bond factor' score. If nothing scores above a threshold, the system creates a new memory node instead of forcing an awkward match.

The patent openly describes 'hallucinated memories.' When a guest's story has no counterpart in the character's backstory, the AI invents one and permanently adds it to the memory bank. Disney frames this as improvisation rather than deception, but it raises real questions about consistency, disclosure, and what happens when a character 'remembers' something that never happened.

A sister patent, filed the same day by an overlapping team, turns the matched memory into a performance. The character selects a song structure, writes lyrics, composes chords and melody, derives a 'mood modifier' from the emotion attached to the memory, then performs the song, poem, or dance. The article notes AI-generated music still lags human composition in quality.

These are patents, not products. Disney has made no announcement, filings are often defensive or exploratory, and deployment could be years away if it happens at all. Disney's recent patent activity instead clusters around motion capture, automated photo cleanup, and the HoloTile Floor, suggesting parallel R&D tracks rather than one imminent launch.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the patents signal that persistent, emotion-weighted memory is becoming the real battleground, not raw model quality. Expect more products built around threshold-triggered memory writes and emotion-conditioned generation. For developers, the architecture is reproducible: vector retrieval over a persona memory store, similarity scoring, fallback insertion, and a mood-modifier layer feeding a generative pipeline. The hard part is governance, since reminiscence data is intimate, often involves children, and blends into biometric and voice data. For regular users, interactions could feel genuinely personal instead of scripted, but also engineered to manufacture attachment. The ethical risk is emotional bonding treated as an engagement metric, with guests unable to tell which memories are real, invented, or retained.
report.tools: To prototype this, try Letta (formerly MemGPT) or Mem0 for persistent agent memory, Zep for long-term conversation stores, and Chroma or FAISS as the vector memory bank. LangGraph handles the elicit-score-threshold-insert loop. For the creative patent, Meta's AudioCraft/MusicGen covers melody generation, with LLM prompt chains for lyrics. Inworld AI and NVIDIA ACE target emotionally expressive game characters. Read Disney's published patents directly via USPTO or Google Patents for the full diagrams.
